L9: # Title:SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Lei Shi】, 【6†Qiuran Lyu】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy, by Lei Shi and 1 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【7†View PDF】 【8†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects---such as text, images, and video---that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target.
L17: We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks.
L18: The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET's performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.

L9: # Title:Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Siqi He】, 【6†Yehua Wei】, 【7†Jiaming Xu】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments, by Siqi He and 2 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【8†View PDF】 【9†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon.
L17: We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy.
L18: The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Nick Arnosti】, 【6†Rad Niazadeh】, 【7†Pranav Nuti】, 【8†Felipe Simon】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies, by Nick Arnosti and 3 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【9†View PDF】 【10†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases.
L17: We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020]
L18: > Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents).
L19: These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.

L8: [Submitted on 20 Aug 2026]
L9: # Title:GenMatch: An End-to-End Generative Matching Framework for Micro-View Order-Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Chuang Liu】, 【6†Yuxueqing Zhang】, 【7†Tengfei Lyu】, 【8†Zirui Yuan】, 【9†Weiqi Hu】, 【10†Yanghan Cheng】, 【11†Ming Wang】, 【12†Li Ma】, 【13†Zihao Lu】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled GenMatch: An End-to-End Generative Matching Framework for Micro-View Order-Dispatching in Ride-Hailing, by Chuang Liu and 7 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【14†View PDF】 【15†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Micro-View Order-Dispatching assigns available drivers to passenger orders within each dispatch batch and is critical to the service quality and operational efficiency of ride-hailing platforms. Mainstream industrial solutions follow a multi-stage paradigm of model prediction, value calculation, and dispatch matching. Although dispatch quality is determined by the final batch-level assignment, these stages optimize different intermediate objectives.
L17: This cross-stage objective inconsistency means that improving a single stage does not necessarily improve the overall dispatch result. We therefore formulate Micro-View Order-Dispatching as a generative matching problem and propose GenMatch, an end-to-end Generative Matching framework and the first such framework deployed in a real-world production environment. Applying generative modeling to this problem introduces three challenges.
L18: First, each dispatch batch forms a dynamic sparse bipartite graph, requiring efficient structured batch-level encoding. Second, replacing the hand-crafted value function requires learning unified business utility from heterogeneous feedback. Third, directly generating an assignment requires tracking the evolving matching state because each selected order-driver pair changes the remaining feasible candidates.
L19: GenMatch addresses these challenges with a Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder, a Business-Aware Utility Learner, and a State-Aware Pointer Decoder. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests in five cities across DiDi's international ride-hailing markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming the effectiveness and practicality of GenMatch for industrial order-dispatching.

L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Xinxing Zhou】, 【6†Xiaojie Yuan】, 【7†Yanlong Wen】, 【8†Ming Jin】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series, by Xinxing Zhou and 3 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【9†View PDF】 【10†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series.
L17: Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision.
L18: We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking.
L19: These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

L9: # Title:Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†L. Jeff Hong】, 【6†Weihuan Huang】, 【7†Xinyao Li】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative, by L. Jeff Hong and 2 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【8†View PDF】 【9†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability.
L17: Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity.
L18: GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

L16: > Abstract:Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better.
L17: When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect.
L18: We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity.
L19: Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

L16: > Abstract:We study steady-state queueing control when decisions must be learned from a single persistent operating trajectory: only the implemented action produces data, and the queue is not reset when the action changes. Fixed-event-count cycles yield a direct ratio-of-totals sample-average approximation (SAA) of each action's steady-state cost rate.
L17: A Top-K coarse-to-fine search ranks these estimates, retains several promising refinement paths, and concentrates later operation on finer candidate sets, without requiring gradients, convexity, or differentiability. We decompose direct-SAA error into accumulated conditional transient bias and martingale fluctuation. For regenerative queues, a bias-function representation reduces transient effects within contiguous action blocks to boundary terms.
L18: Finite-sample stagewise bounds then link estimation accuracy to master-grid identification through guardian retention, and the required queueing and sampling conditions are verified for a persistent-workload M/M/1 implementation. At a common active set, Top-K has a weakly larger guardian margin than Top-1, and an exact-objective example shows Top-1 can discard the optimal refinement branch.
L19: Numerical experiments delineate scope rather than universal dominance: Top-K improves terminal identification in the reported LiQUAR and mixed staffing comparisons, while LiQUAR can have lower cumulative learning cost, and GOLiQ is markedly stronger on a smooth benchmark with reliable queueing sensitivities. Direct ranking is therefore best viewed as a complementary method when model-specific gradients are unavailable, inconvenient, or poorly matched to the decision space.
